extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, policymakers, scholars, and law students interested in AI and intellectual property law
extracted.subtask_description: Legal and policy analysis of how existing U.S. patent and copyright doctrines apply to AI-related technologies, AI-generated inventions, and issues of inventorship, liability, prior art, and examination. Discusses statutory tests (35 U.S.C. §101), case law (Alice and related cases), and policy proposals for reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter under 35 U.S.C. §101
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of patentable subject matter is confined to any 'new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof.' This provision excludes from patent eligibility those claims that pertain to abstract concepts (such as mathematical formulas), naturally occurring phenomena, or fundamental scientific principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court justification: such ideas are building blocks of scientific and technological progress and granting exclusivity could obstruct innovation (citing Mayo). Use §101 analysis to screen out abstract ideas before substantive patentability inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice framework / inventive concept requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that describe activities capable of being executed by 'an ordinary mental process,' 'within the human mind,' or 'by an individual using pen and paper' are generally rejected as abstract unless they demonstrate a distinct technological advancement beyond tasks typically done manually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Alice, claims must exhibit an 'inventive concept' to be patent-eligible. Courts require more than applying an abstract idea on a standard computer; claims should show concrete improvement in computer-related technology. Examples: Purepredictive (predictive analytics patent invalidated as abstract) and Blue Spike (claims dismissed as general application of an abstract idea).

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of Alice to AI-based software
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2014 tightening of patentable subject matter made patenting software and 'computer-implemented inventions' significantly more rigorous, which poses obstacles for AI-related patents because AI often replicates human cognitive functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because AI is designed to replicate cognitive/human tasks, many AI-related claims face heightened scrutiny under Alice; applicants should emphasize concrete technological improvements, not mere automation of human tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent eligibility of AI-generated inventions (whether AI-originated creations can be patented)
rubrics_metrics.description: Open question whether inventions generated by artificial intelligence qualify for patent protection and, if so, who rightfully qualifies as the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unresolved in U.S. law; some patents have been granted for inventions attributed to AI systems in practice. Policy analysis should weigh whether such protection advances patent law objectives (innovation, disclosure) and consider alternative mechanisms (trade secret, public recognition) if patents are inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship requires 'conception' by a natural person
rubrics_metrics.description: Conception—defined as the mental act of forming a definite and enduring idea of a working invention—constitutes a core requirement, and this act must be carried out by a natural person. Judicial interpretations have consistently stated that only individual human beings can fulfill this cognitive function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory language and practice reinforce human-centered inventorship: Section 101 refers to 'whoever' invents, Section 102 uses 'person', and applications require an inventor's declaration/oath. Federal Circuit precedent construes these requirements narrowly to require human inventors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Options for assigning inventorship for AI-originated inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: If conceptual inventive acts occur entirely within an AI system, two fundamental options arise: (1) assign inventorship to the AI system itself, or (2) omit listing any inventor on the patent document (requiring statutory revision).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assigning inventorship to AI would require granting legal entity/personhood to AI; omitting inventors would require creating mechanisms to preserve incentives (e.g., assignee rights, new categories for AI developers). Policymakers must assess whether either option produces meaningful benefits versus harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve incentives for developers/operators when AI inventions are patented
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the owner appears as assignee, individual engineers and developers who enable AI-generated inventions often remain unacknowledged on the patent record; this can undermine incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider creating a new patent-system category to recognize AI developers or other mechanisms (contractual arrangements, assignment regimes) so contributors receive appropriate credit and incentives to continue development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raise nonobviousness threshold or differentiate patent terms based on human contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy proposals include increasing the threshold of patentability (e.g., elevating nonobviousness standards) for inventions created entirely by AI, or assigning differentiated patent terms according to the extent of human contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such changes aim to balance competition between human inventors and machine-generated inventions; they require safeguards (e.g., truthful disclosure of AI involvement) to prevent exploitation of the system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit patent protection to socially valuable AI inventions / tighten utility requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: One reform possibility is lowering the eligibility threshold for AI inventions only in fields with high social value, or tightening the utility requirement under 35 U.S.C. §101 so that only AI inventions with significant usefulness qualify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to historical 'moral utility' reasoning denying patents for socially objectionable items; proposals would restrict patents to areas like medicine, environmental sustainability, criminal justice, and education. Policymakers must balance public benefit against stifling innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability allocation for AI-caused patent infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent infringement analysis currently involves claim construction and proving that accused technology fulfills each claim element (or equivalents); induced infringement holds liable those who knowingly aid direct infringement. U.S. statutes do not contemplate autonomous AI committing infringement without human oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unclear how to assign accountability when AI independently infringes. Options include holding users, developers/manufacturers, owners, or AI itself liable. Any regime should consider deterrence, fairness, foreseeability, and effects on innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradeoffs in assigning liability to users versus developers
rubrics_metrics.description: User liability derives from traditional doctrines holding product users responsible for damage caused by their use; developer liability treats developers/producers as responsible because they can predict and prevent violations and benefit from commercialization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: User liability may be unfair where users lack technical ability to foresee infringements; developers are often targeted in practice and may provide indemnities. Extending product-liability analogies to AI could justify holding manufacturers responsible for AI 'malfunctions' that infringe patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Granting legal personhood to AI for liability purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative is to assign liability to AI itself by granting it legal personhood (e.g., 'electronic persons') for highly autonomous agents, enabling them to bear legal responsibility for damages caused by their actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: European Parliament has proposed classifying highly autonomous robots as 'electronic persons.' Granting personhood may be easier to justify for liability than inventorship, but raises deep normative and practical issues about rights, duties, and enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insurance, compensation funds, and contractual allocation of AI risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed pragmatic solutions include compulsory insurance (analogous to auto insurance), compensation funds to cover uninsured harms, and contractual liability allocations (indemnity clauses) among parties in the AI deployment chain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These mechanisms can spread risk and ensure recovery even where a responsible party is hard to identify; however, they must be tailored to include all relevant actors (manufacturers, trainers, deployers) and avoid chilling innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redefinition of Person of Ordinary Skill in the Art (POSITA)
rubrics_metrics.description: With AI integration, stakeholders must consider whether POSITA should remain a human or be redefined to include a human using AI or AI alone; such a change would raise the threshold for non-obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expanding POSITA to include AI could make many human inventions obvious (if AI benchmark is superintelligent), risk excluding meritorious human innovations, and potentially render conventional patent incentives less effective. Policymakers should carefully evaluate trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulating AI-drafted patent applications and USPTO capacity concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: If AI systems can independently draft patent applications and submit filings en masse, the USPTO may be overwhelmed; there may be a need for specific regulations governing AI-submitted applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible mitigations include increasing filing and administrative fees to deter low-quality submissions, and revising procedures to manage volume while preserving examination quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of AI-generated content as prior art and disclosure obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate over whether AI-generated content should be accepted as prior art; if accepted, it could complicate prior art searches and make applicants' duty to disclose material prior art harder to fulfill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excluding AI-generated prior art for practical reasons may conflict with foundational policies of patent disclosure and examination. A balance is needed between administrative feasibility and legal principles ensuring examiners see the best prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of ethical, societal, and economic impacts (first-mover advantage, labor displacement, inequality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reforms must assess whether lowering eligibility thresholds or otherwise changing patent law would disproportionately benefit incumbent AI firms, risk concentrating control, exacerbate inequality, and have distinct labor-market impacts compared to past technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy proposals should weigh potential benefits (accelerated breakthroughs) against harms (monopolization, displacement of human creativity), and consider targeted reforms (e.g., limiting protection to socially beneficial fields) to mitigate negative consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of natural person authorship in copyright
rubrics_metrics.description: Under copyright law, authorship generally requires a natural person; many jurisdictions refrain from granting copyright to works produced with minimal or no human involvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two legal approaches when dealing with AI-only works: exclude such works from copyright eligibility, or assign authorship to the human who developed or used the AI. Copyright rules and registration practices (e.g., U.S. Copyright Office) tend to presuppose human authorship.
